1.definition: Theodora Kantakouzene, daughter of the Byzantine claimant John Kantakouzenos, given in marriage to Orhan in 1346 — a Christian Byzantine princess wed to a Muslim Turkic sultan as the price of military aid in a Byzantine civil war.

2.definition: Yakub Çelebi, younger son of Murad I, strangled by his brother Bayezid on the battlefield of Kosovo in 1389 — an early instance of the Ottoman fratricidal succession that Mehmed II would later codify into law.
Yeñiçeri ("new troops"), the Ottoman Turkish term that gave English the word "Janissary" — the sultan's standing slave-soldier infantry corps created under Murad I.

3.definition: Timur-i Lang ("Timur the Lame"), the Persian nickname behind the European name "Tamerlane" — a reference to the permanent battlefield injury of the Central Asian conqueror who destroyed Bayezid I's army at Ankara in 1402.

The first real Ottoman gunpowder artillery — heavy bombards thrown against the Theodosian Walls in the failed 1422 siege — proved, even in failure, that cannon could one day breach the masonry that had protected Constantinople for a thousand years.

4.definition: The Basilica (Ottoman Şahi), the colossal bronze bombard cast by the Hungarian gun-founder Orban for the 1453 siege — its barrel reportedly twenty-seven feet long, throwing a stone ball of around twelve hundred pounds; the largest cannon the world had yet seen.

Eis tēn polin, Greek for "into the city" — the colloquial phrase Greek speakers used for going to Constantinople, which over centuries was corrupted into the parallel popular name "Istanbul," standardized as official only in 1930.

5.definition: Yavuz ("the Stern" or "the Grim"), the Ottoman epithet for Selim I — the short-reigning but transformative sultan who doubled the empire, crushed the Mamluks, and claimed the Caliphate between 1512 and 1520.

Sufi communities — adherents of Islam's mystical orders — formed one of the many heterodox religious populations within the Ottoman pluralist order alongside Sunni, Christian, Jewish and Druze subjects.

Kanuni ("the Lawgiver"), the Ottoman epithet for Süleyman the Magnificent — earned by his comprehensive codification of secular imperial law (kanun) that his jurist Ebussuud Efendi harmonized with the sharia.

6.definition: The first devshirme stream: the most physically capable but less academically promising boys were placed for several years with Turkish village families in Anatolia to learn Turkish, Islam, and farming before induction into the Janissary corps.

7.definition: Cecilia Venier-Baffo, the Venetian-Greek noblewoman born on Paros who, captured by corsairs, rose through the harem to become Nurbanu Sultan — favored consort of Selim II and one of the great valide sultans of the Sultanate of Women.

Anastasia, the Greek priest's daughter from Tinos captured around age fifteen who, as Kösem Sultan, became the most powerful figure in the seventeenth-century Ottoman Empire for nearly three decades until her assassination in 1651.

Mehmed Pasha Köprülü (c. 1575–1661), the eighty-one-year-old Albanian-devshirme grand vizier appointed in 1656 on conditions he dictated — full authority, the right to confiscate, immunity from harem interference — who halted the empire's administrative drift and founded the Köprülü vizieral dynasty.

8.definition: The Cihannüma ("Universal Geography"), Ibrahim Müteferrika's most famous publication — a comprehensive geographical reference incorporating recent European cartographic knowledge, printed at the first Ottoman Arabic-script press.

9.definition: The Imperial Engineering School, one of the European-modeled technical academies Mahmud II founded after destroying the Janissaries — part of the institutional groundwork for the Tanzimat reforms.

10.definition: "The Red Sultan" — the European epithet for Abdülhamid II, the autocrat blamed for the suppression of the Ottoman press, a vast secret-police network, and the Hamidian Massacres of Armenian Christians in 1894–1896.
The Imperial Naval School, one of the European-modeled professional academies of Abdülhamid II's reign that produced the technocratic, European-educated officer class which became the Young Turks.

The Military Medical School in Istanbul — the institution where medical students founded the Committee of Union and Progress in 1889, seeding the Young Turk movement that ended Abdülhamid II's autocracy.

The Russian Caucasus — the Transcaucasian territories under Russian rule whose Armenian communities supported the eastern-Anatolian Armenian nationalist movements that Abdülhamid II viewed as an existential threat.

11.definition: The Russian Caucasus — the Transcaucasian territories under Russian rule where a substantial Armenian population lived, distinct from the Ottoman Armenian community of eastern Anatolia destroyed in the genocide.
Soviet Armenia, the Armenian Soviet republic established after the war that became the modern Republic of Armenia — home, with the diaspora, to much of the surviving Armenian population.

12.matchText: Islamic State of Iraq and Syria

12.definition: Kayser-i Rûm ("Caesar of Rome"), the title Mehmed II adopted after 1453 — the Ottoman claim to be the legitimate continuation of the Roman imperial tradition, parallel to Russia's "Third Rome" doctrine.
The Sufi tariqats — organized mystical brotherhoods such as the Mevlevi, Bektashi and Naqshbandi orders, embedded in Ottoman religious life for centuries and formally banned by the Republic in 1925.

The "Caliphate question" — the unresolved theological-political problem, dormant since Atatürk's 1924 abolition, of how pan-Islamic religious leadership should be institutionally embodied in Sunni Islam.
